subject: Banking
title: Derivatives and Synthetic Risk
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Derivatives and Synthetic Risk.

hook.text: A derivative is a financial contract whose value depends on something else.

buildup.text: Options, futures, and swaps let traders bet on price movements without owning the underlying asset. Pure risk transfer.

discovery.text: Companies use derivatives to hedge real risks. Airlines buy fuel futures to lock in prices.

twist.text: Speculators dominate derivatives markets. Warren Buffett called them financial weapons of mass destruction.

climax.text: Derivatives can protect or destroy. The same tool hedges airline fuel costs and nearly collapsed the economy in 2008.

punchline.text: $600 trillion market. Protection and destruction share the same tool.

quiz.question: What did Warren Buffett famously call derivatives?

details.summary: Derivatives are financial contracts whose value depends on an underlying asset like a stock, bond, or commodity. Investment banks create, trade, and sell these instruments, generating enormous profits but also concentrating systemic risk.
details.whyItMatters: The global derivatives market is estimated at over 600 trillion dollars in notional value. Derivatives amplified the 2008 crisis by spreading mortgage risk throughout the financial system in ways nobody fully understood.
takeaways: Derivatives derive their value from underlying assets or benchmarks
The notional value of global derivatives exceeds 600 trillion dollars
Credit default swaps on mortgages were central to the 2008 financial crisis

faq.question: What is a derivative in simple terms?
faq.answer: A derivative is a bet on the future price of something. An oil futures contract, for example, locks in a price for oil delivery next month. You profit if the actual price is higher, and lose if it is lower.

faq.question: How did derivatives cause the 2008 crisis?
faq.answer: Banks bundled risky mortgages into securities, then sold credit default swaps insuring those securities. When mortgages defaulted, every institution that sold swaps owed money simultaneously, creating a chain reaction that nearly collapsed the system.
